#### Statistical distributions

- How is a standard normal random variable represented?
  - $Z\sim N(0,1)$
- What are the mean and variance of a standard normal random variable:
  - Mean?
    - $0$
  - Variance?
    - $1$
- Chi-squared distribution:
  - How is a central chi-squared random variable with $n$ degrees of freedom constructed?
    - As the sum of squares of $n$ independent standard normal random variables
  - What distributional conditions must the random variables satisfy:
    - First?
      - $Z_i\sim N(0,1)$
    - Second?
      - They are independent
  - What is the defining relationship?
    - $X^2=\sum_{i=1}^n Z_i^2\sim\chi_n^2$
  - What is its expected value?
    - $\mathrm{E}(X^2)=n$
  - What is its variance?
    - $\mathrm{Var}(X^2)=2n$
- How can independent non-standard normal variables be used to construct a chi-squared random variable:
  - What is assumed about each variable?
    - $Y_i\sim N(\mu_i,\sigma_i^2)$
  - How must the variables relate?
    - They must be independent
  - How is each variable standardised?
    - $\frac{Y_i-\mu_i}{\sigma_i}$
  - What is the resulting relationship?
    - $X^2=\sum_{i=1}^n\left(\frac{Y_i-\mu_i}{\sigma_i}\right)^2\sim\chi_n^2$
- How can a multivariate normal random vector be used to construct a chi-squared random variable:
  - What is the distribution of the random vector?
    - $\symbf{Y}\sim\mathrm{MVN}(\symbf{\mu},\symbf{\Sigma})$
  - What dimension does the random vector have?
    - $n$
  - What condition is imposed on the covariance matrix?
    - It is positive definite
  - What consequence does positive definiteness have here?
    - The covariance matrix is invertible
  - What is the resulting relationship?
    - $(\symbf{Y}-\symbf{\mu})^T\symbf{\Sigma}^{-1}(\symbf{Y}-\symbf{\mu})\sim\chi_n^2$
- $t$-distribution:
  - How is a $t$ random variable with $n$ degrees of freedom defined?
    - $T=\frac{Z}{\sqrt{X^2/n}}\sim t_n$
  - What is the distribution of the numerator?
    - $Z\sim N(0,1)$
  - What is the distribution of the chi-squared variable in the denominator?
    - $X^2\sim\chi_n^2$
  - How must the numerator and chi-squared variable relate?
    - They must be independent
- $F$-distribution:
  - How is an $F$ random variable with $n$ and $m$ degrees of freedom defined?
    - $F=\frac{X_1^2/n}{X_2^2/m}\sim F_{n,m}$
  - What is the distribution of the numerator's chi-squared variable?
    - $X_1^2\sim\chi_n^2$
  - What is the distribution of the denominator's chi-squared variable?
    - $X_2^2\sim\chi_m^2$
  - How must the two chi-squared variables relate?
    - They must be independent
- How are the $t$- and $F$-distributions related?
  - Squaring a $t_n$ random variable produces an $F_{1,n}$ random variable
- What is the relationship in symbols?
  - $T\sim t_n\implies T^2\sim F_{1,n}$

#### Linear algebra

- Row and column notation:
  - What does $\symbf{a}_{[i]}$ refer to?
    - The $i$-th row of $\symbf{A}$
  - How is that row written when considered outside the matrix?
    - As a column vector
  - What does $\symbf{a}_i$ refer to?
    - The $i$-th column of $\symbf{A}$
  - How is that column written when considered outside the matrix?
    - As a column vector
- For $\symbf{A}=\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\3&4\end{bmatrix}$, what is its first row under the course convention?
  - $\symbf{a}_{[1]}=\begin{bmatrix}1\\2\end{bmatrix}$
- For the same matrix, what is its first column?
  - $\symbf{a}_1=\begin{bmatrix}1\\3\end{bmatrix}$
- Why is a row written as a column vector when it is discussed on its own?
  - This is the adopted vector-notation convention
- May the notes and slides sometimes deviate from this convention?
  - Yes
- Matrix multiplication:
  - How is the $ij$-th element of $\symbf{AB}$ calculated?
    - As the dot product of the $i$-th row of $\symbf{A}$ and the $j$-th column of $\symbf{B}$
  - What is the formula using transpose notation?
    - $(\symbf{AB})_{ij}=\symbf{a}_{[i]}'\symbf{b}_j$
  - What is the equivalent dot-product notation?
    - $(\symbf{AB})_{ij}=\symbf{a}_{[i]}\cdot\symbf{b}_j$
- Block matrix multiplication:
  - When can block matrix multiplication be especially useful?
    - When submatrices have useful structure
  - How are submatrices treated during block multiplication?
    - Like elements in ordinary matrix multiplication
  - What condition must the blocks satisfy?
    - They must be conformable
  - What does conformable mean in this context?
    - Their dimensions line up so that the multiplications are defined
  - Which structured matrices can simplify block multiplication:
    - First?
      - Identity matrices
    - Second?
      - Zero matrices
  - Why can block multiplication be easier than writing every dot product?
    - It exploits the effects of identity and zero matrices
  - Where will this block structure later be useful?
    - In factorising idempotent matrices
- Orthogonal vectors:
  - What is the algebraic condition for two vectors to be orthogonal?
    - $\symbf{x}^T\symbf{y}=\sum_i x_i y_i=0$
  - What is the equivalent geometric condition?
    - The angle between them is 90 degrees
- Give an example of two orthogonal vectors.
  $\begin{bmatrix}1\\2\end{bmatrix}\text{ and }\begin{bmatrix}-2\\1\end{bmatrix}$
- What makes a set of vectors orthonormal:
  - First?
    - The vectors are mutually orthogonal
  - Second?
    - Every vector has unit length
- Orthogonal matrices:
  - What shape must an orthogonal matrix have?
    - It must be square
  - What defining identity does an orthogonal matrix satisfy?
    - $\symbf{Q}'\symbf{Q}=\symbf{Q}\symbf{Q}'=\symbf{I}$
  - What equivalent property do its columns have?
    - They form an orthonormal set
  - What property do its rows then also have?
    - They form an orthonormal set
  - Why can the term "orthogonal matrix" be confusing?
    - Its columns are orthonormal, not merely orthogonal
  - How is its inverse calculated?
    - $\symbf{Q}^{-1}=\symbf{Q}'$
- Is the identity matrix orthogonal?
  - Yes
- When is a diagonal matrix orthogonal?
  - When every diagonal entry is either 1 or -1
- Why is $\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\0&2\end{bmatrix}$ not an orthogonal matrix?
  - Its second column does not have unit length
- What property does $\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\0&2\end{bmatrix}$ nevertheless have?
  - Its columns are orthogonal
- What must be done to mutually orthogonal columns that do not have unit length before they form an orthogonal matrix?
  - They must be normalised
- Where do orthogonal matrices appear in this course:
  - First?
    - In the factorisation of real symmetric matrices
  - Second?
    - In the factorisation of symmetric idempotent matrices
- In regression, to which vector is the residual vector orthogonal?
  - The vector of fitted values
- In regression, to which matrix columns is the residual vector orthogonal?
  - The columns of the model matrix
- What are the relevant regression vectors?
  - $\symbf{e}=\symbf{y}-\hat{\symbf{y}}$
- Trace:
  - How is the trace of a matrix calculated?
    - By summing its diagonal elements
  - What is the trace of $\begin{bmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{bmatrix}$?
    - $a+d$
- For $\symbf{A}:p\times q$ and $\symbf{B}:q\times p$, what trace identity holds?
  - $\mathrm{tr}(\symbf{A}\symbf{B})=\mathrm{tr}(\symbf{B}\symbf{A})$
- Cyclic trace property:
  - What identity holds for conformable matrices $\symbf{A}$, $\symbf{B}$ and $\symbf{C}$?
    - $\mathrm{tr}(\symbf{A}\symbf{B}\symbf{C})=\mathrm{tr}(\symbf{C}\symbf{A}\symbf{B})=\mathrm{tr}(\symbf{B}\symbf{C}\symbf{A})$
  - Does the cyclic trace property permit arbitrary reordering?
    - No
  - Which reordered expression is not generally equal to $\mathrm{tr}(\symbf{A}\symbf{B}\symbf{C})$?
    - $\mathrm{tr}(\symbf{B}\symbf{A}\symbf{C})$
- Rank:
  - How can rank be described in terms of a basis?
    - As the size of a basis of the column or row space
  - What is a basis?
    - A minimal set of vectors that spans the relevant space
  - How can rank be described in terms of linear independence?
    - As the number of linearly independent columns or rows
- Full rank:
  - Under the terminology used in these notes, when is a matrix called full rank?
    - When it is square and its rank equals its number of rows and columns
  - For an $n\times n$ matrix, what is the full-rank condition?
    - $\mathrm{rank}(\symbf{A})=n$
  - What key implication follows for a full-rank square matrix?
    - Its inverse exists
  - What inverse identity then holds?
    - $\symbf{A}\symbf{A}^{-1}=\symbf{I}$
- What is the maximum possible rank of a rectangular matrix?
  - The smaller of its number of rows and columns
- When does a rectangular matrix have full column rank?
  - When its rank equals its number of columns
- When does a rectangular matrix have full row rank?
  - When its rank equals its number of rows
- Which matrices have the same rank as $\symbf{A}$?
  - $\symbf{A}',\ \symbf{A}\symbf{A}',\ \text{and }\symbf{A}'\symbf{A}$
- Under what condition do the product-rank equalities apply?
  - The relevant products must exist
- Why is the rank of $\symbf{X}'\symbf{X}$ relevant in this course?
  - A centred data matrix produces a covariance matrix proportional to $\symbf{X}'\symbf{X}$
- Eigenvectors and eigenvalues:
  - What is an eigenvector $\symbf{x}$ of a matrix $\symbf{A}$?
    - A non-zero vector whose direction is unchanged by multiplication by $\symbf{A}$
  - What equation defines it?
    - $\symbf{A}\symbf{x}=\lambda\symbf{x}$
  - What does $\lambda$ represent?
    - The corresponding eigenvalue
  - Is an eigenvector required by definition to have unit length?
    - No
  - What happens when an eigenvector is multiplied by a non-zero scalar?
    - It remains an eigenvector for the same eigenvalue
  - Why are eigenvectors conventionally normalised?
    - Their scale is otherwise arbitrary
  - What length convention is used in this course?
    - Unit length
- Symmetric matrices:
  - What condition defines a symmetric matrix?
    - $\symbf{A}=\symbf{A}'$
  - What shape must a symmetric matrix have?
    - It must be square
  - How can any real symmetric matrix be factorised?
    - $\symbf{A}=\symbf{P}\symbf{\Lambda}\symbf{P}'$
  - What are the columns of $\symbf{P}$?
    - An orthonormal set of eigenvectors of $\symbf{A}$
  - What kind of matrix is $\symbf{P}$?
    - An orthogonal matrix
  - What does $\symbf{\Lambda}$ contain?
    - The ordered eigenvalues of $\symbf{A}$
  - What kind of matrix is $\symbf{\Lambda}$?
    - A diagonal matrix
- Positive definite matrices:
  - What two properties define a positive definite matrix:
    - First?
      - It is symmetric
    - Second?
      - All its eigenvalues are positive
  - What equivalent quadratic-form condition holds for every non-zero vector $\symbf{x}$?
    - $\symbf{x}'\symbf{A}\symbf{x}>0$
- Positive semidefinite matrices:
  - What quadratic-form condition defines a symmetric positive semidefinite matrix?
    - $\symbf{x}'\symbf{A}\symbf{x}\geq0\text{ for every }\symbf{x}$
  - Must all its eigenvalues be strictly positive?
    - No
- Why is every covariance matrix positive semidefinite?
  - Every linear combination has non-negative variance
- What identity establishes this result?
  - $\symbf{a}'\symbf{\Sigma}\symbf{a}=\mathrm{Var}(\symbf{a}'\symbf{X})\geq0$
- When is a covariance matrix positive definite?
  - When every non-zero linear combination of the variables has positive variance
- What prevents a covariance matrix from being positive definite?
  - An exact linear dependency among the variables
- Idempotent matrices:
  - What condition defines an idempotent matrix?
    - $\symbf{A}^2=\symbf{A}$
  - What values can its eigenvalues take?
    - $0\text{ or }1$
  - Must both eigenvalues occur?
    - No
  - How can a general idempotent matrix be diagonalised?
    - $\symbf{A}=\symbf{P}\symbf{\Lambda}\symbf{P}^{-1}$
  - When can an idempotent matrix be orthogonally diagonalised?
    - When it is also symmetric
  - What is the orthogonal diagonalisation in that case?
    - $\symbf{A}=\symbf{P}\symbf{\Lambda}\symbf{P}'$
  - What kind of matrix is $\symbf{P}$ in the symmetric case?
    - An orthogonal matrix
  - What is the block form of $\symbf{\Lambda}$ in the symmetric case?
    - $\symbf{\Lambda}=\begin{bmatrix}\symbf{I}_r&0\\0&0\end{bmatrix}$
  - What does $r$ represent?
    - $r=\mathrm{rank}(\symbf{A})$
  - What is $\symbf{I}_r$?
    - The $r\times r$ identity matrix
  - If $\symbf{A}$ is idempotent, what related matrix is also idempotent?
    - $\symbf{I}-\symbf{A}$
- Where do idempotent matrices occur in regression:
  - What is the hat matrix?
    - $\symbf{H}=\symbf{X}(\symbf{X}'\symbf{X})^{-1}\symbf{X}'$
  - Which two special properties does the hat matrix have:
    - First?
      - It is symmetric
    - Second?
      - It is idempotent
  - How are fitted values calculated using the hat matrix?
    - $\hat{\symbf{y}}=\symbf{H}\symbf{y}$
  - What is the residual-maker matrix?
    - $\symbf{I}-\symbf{H}$
  - How are residuals calculated using it?
    - $\symbf{e}=(\symbf{I}-\symbf{H})\symbf{y}$
  - What orthogonality result do these properties help establish?
    - Residuals are orthogonal to fitted values
